focus: Angle 9: Prior art. Compare explicit slash command catalogs, metadata-driven plain-language skill activation, evaluation practice and host-specific invocation constraints.
noveltyJustification: Four findings add primary-source prior art and map its activation/evaluation patterns to this repository; one extends the runtime-specific limitation already identified.
keyQuestions: Which one canonical inventory reconciles command metadata, active bridge allow-list rows and doctor routing declarations for all 45 slash commands?
How should command intent and skill intent combine so plain planning and research prompts reach the matching workflow with acceptable recall and precision?
What should a command recommendation show, and which commands can the model invoke directly versus asking first?
How does a plain chat request reach the appropriate command workflow across supported runtimes, and how should skills link to command front doors?
What benchmark evidence, prior art and failure controls should validate the design?
ruledOut: Adding a static table of all commands to every fallback; the strategy marks universal fallback guidance BLOCKED.
Assuming every runtime has an API to invoke slash commands from model context; the strategy marks this BLOCKED after the DSH evidence.

label: GitHub Copilot’s app documents a typed slash picker, commands that invoke skills and workflows, and context/session-dependent command availability; this supports a visible, runtime-owned picker with direct command aliases, while the context caveat contradicts assuming one universal static slash surface.

OpenAI’s skill pattern exposes name and description metadata first, then loads the workflow when the request matches or the user invokes it directly; repository command metadata already carries user-goal signals and ordered parent/leaf resources, supporting plain chat and explicit command paths that converge on one workflow identity.

OpenAI’s skill-evaluation guidance tests both intended activation and unwanted activation, includes direct and natural-language prompts, and suggests 10–20 prompts as an early single-skill set; this supports positive and negative gold examples, but does not justify using a small pilot set as proof for all 45 commands or every adapter.

Repository policy separates skill routing from command workflow and write approval: Gate 2 chooses/loads the skill, Gate 4 gives the command workflow precedence over executor transport, and Gate 3 or an action contract can still require a question; the hook itself is advisory and fail-open. This contradicts treating an advisor match as permission to execute.

Prior art and local adapters support one runtime-neutral route contract with host-specific invocation: explicit slash input resolves exactly, plain-language descriptions resolve the same packaged workflow, then the workflow’s action policy decides run or ask. Copilot’s commands are context-bound, the local adapters use different delivery channels, and DSH has no command loader, so no source supports assuming every runtime can invoke the same slash API.
